claims.text: The stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by a temperature-dependent interplay between lattice distortion and phase stability.
Temperature-dependent lattice distortion and phase stability modulate the alloy's thermal expansion.
Temperature-dependent lattice distortion and phase stability modulate elastic-modulus anisotropy.
Changes in thermal expansion and elastic-modulus anisotropy generate thermal stresses during composite solidification.
The material is to be tested in a homogenized state before further thermal or mechanical processing.
Thermal expansion coefficients and elastic-modulus anisotropy will be measured from 293 K to 1250 K.
Thermal expansion and elastic-modulus measurements will be correlated with stress–strain behavior under controlled thermal cycling and mechanical loading.
Controlled thermal cycling and mechanical loading over 293–1250 K can simulate conditions relevant to composite solidification.
Variations in lattice distortion with temperature alter the thermal expansion coefficient.
Variations in phase stability with temperature alter elastic-modulus anisotropy.
The resulting thermal stresses influence stress–strain behavior.
Thermal expansion coefficients will exhibit significant temperature dependence.
Elastic-modulus anisotropy will exhibit significant temperature dependence.
Thermal-stress generation will increase at higher temperatures.
Deviations in stress–strain behavior will become pronounced above approximately 800 K.
At 293 K, thermal-stress generation is minimal.
High-temperature XRD can be used to measure lattice parameters and derive thermal expansion coefficients across the specified temperature range.
Ultrasonic measurements can determine elastic-modulus anisotropy across the specified temperature range.
A lack of significant temperature dependence in thermal expansion or elastic-modulus anisotropy would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between stress–strain behavior and predicted thermal-stress generation would falsify the hypothesis.
